The Sinai Peninsula. A triangular landmass connecting Africa to Asia, bordered by the Mediterranean Sea to the north, the Red Sea to the east and south, and Egypt to the west. It is one of the most strategically consequential geographies in the world, linking three continents and two religious traditions while hosting one of the planet's most vital shipping lanes.

The peninsula bridges Africa and Asia, and control of it determines access between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean via the Suez Canal. It is predominantly desert—the Negev Desert extends into it—supporting only sparse nomadic populations historically. But its religious significance vastly exceeds its population. Mount Sinai is where, according to biblical tradition, Moses received the Ten Commandments, making the mountain sacred to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam alike.

In modern history, Israel occupied the peninsula during the nineteen sixty-seven Six-Day War, and it was returned to Egypt in stages following the Yom Kippur War, with the process completed by nineteen eighty-two. Today it remains a flashpoint of Israeli-Palestinian tensions and serves as a route for smuggling between Egypt and Gaza. Saint Catherine's Monastery, one of Christianity's oldest surviving monastic communities, is nestled at Mount Sinai's base. The Red Sea separates the peninsula from Saudi Arabia, making it a crossroads of three continents' trade and geopolitics. Its control has shaped empires from Pharaonic Egypt through Ottoman rule to the modern nation-states that govern it today.
